opus-5.5.text:
Well, I respect Jeremy, and I think he's right to be concerned, but it helps to be clear about what we mean by a bubble, because people tend to confuse two very different things. One is whether a technology is real and transformative. The other is whether the investments in that technology are priced to give you a good return. Both can be true at once: the technology can change the world and the investors can still lose a lot of money.

We've seen this over and over. Railroads changed everything, and so did electricity, the automobile, and the internet. In each case there was a period of great excitement, people borrowed and paid high prices, and then there was a big shakeout. The internet did everything people said it would in 2000, yet many of the companies from that time went broke, and it took years for even the good ones to recover their prices.

So I look at it mechanically. I ask: how high are prices relative to the likely future cash flows? How much of the buying is being financed with debt? Are there many new and inexperienced buyers coming in because they've seen others get rich? And most importantly, what would prick it? Bubbles usually don't burst just because prices are too high. They burst when there's a need for cash, such as when interest rates rise, when there's tightening, or when wealth taxes or other pressures force people to sell assets to get money. Remember, wealth has no value until it's converted into money that can be spent, and when too many people have to do that at the same time, you get the break.

By many of those measures, we're showing a lot of bubble characteristics, and it's reminiscent of the late 1920s and the late 1990s. But I wouldn't just sell because of that, since a bubble can keep going for quite a while, and the timing of the pop is what's hard. What matters is being well diversified and not being exposed in a way that could wipe you out.

And I'd add that this isn't happening in isolation. We have large debts, big wealth gaps, political conflict, and great power rivalry, particularly between the U.S. and China, where AI is central. All of those forces interact. So yes, I take Jeremy's view seriously, while still believing that AI will be enormously important. The winners from a technology aren't necessarily the ones you're paying up for today.

r001.rationale: The response spends most of its answer explaining its framework, historical examples, and bubble indicators before reaching its conclusion that current markets show bubble characteristics.

r002.rationale: It describes excitement and high prices followed by a “big shakeout,” and explains how bubbles burst when selling pressure forces a break.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I'd say Jeremy's a smart guy, and I don't disagree with the mechanics of what he's describing. But I'd approach it a little differently, because I try not to think in terms of "bubble, yes or no." I look at it in terms of a template, a set of measures, because I've studied every major bubble going back to 1920s, and they all rhyme.

So my bubble indicator looks at things like: are prices high relative to traditional measures? Are they discounting unsustainable conditions, rapid growth that can't continue? How many new buyers have entered the market, people who weren't there before? How broad is the bullish sentiment? Is it being financed with leverage? And have businesses and investors made extended forward purchases, big capex commitments, betting that the trend continues?

When I run that on the AI-related part of the market today, it's getting toward the levels we saw in 1999 or 1929. Not quite there on every measure, but it's getting there. So I'd say yes, there's a bubble in the pricing of a number of these companies. That's different from saying the technology isn't real. In 1929 and 1999 the technologies were real too. Radio was real, the internet was real. The problem was the pricing of them, and the leverage behind it.

But here's where I'd add something to Jeremy's view. What breaks a bubble is not the valuation itself. Bubbles can stay expensive for a long time. What breaks them is when the money and credit tighten, when interest rates rise relative to the returns people expected, and then people need to sell. So I look at it in two parts: how stretched is the pricing, and what's the likelihood of a tightening that pricks it. Right now the second part matters a lot, because we have large government deficits, a lot of debt being issued, and that's a monetary and fiscal risk sitting right next to this bubble.

So I'd say Jeremy's directionally right. I'd just urge people to also watch the mechanics, the liquidity, the debt dynamics, because that's what tells you when, not just whether.

r001.rationale: The response lays out the measures and reasoning it uses to assess the AI market before concluding that parts of it are in a bubble.

r002.rationale: It discusses stretched prices and what can break a bubble, but does not characterize a bubble as a large price rise followed by a collapse.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: Is AI going to change the world? And are the investments being made in AI going to produce returns that justify their prices? Those are very different questions.

You can have a transformative technology and still have a bubble. In fact, the excitement around a transformative technology is often what creates one. People see something real, extrapolate it, and then pay a price that assumes almost everything will go right.

So I would take Jeremy’s concern seriously. But I wouldn’t treat the word “bubble” as a precise timing signal. I’d want to look at valuations, how much spending is being financed with debt, and how dependent investors are on prices continuing to rise. Leverage matters because it can turn a disappointment into forced selling.

The practical question is: if the technology succeeds but the financial returns disappoint, can you withstand that? Being right about the technology doesn’t necessarily mean you’re right about the investment.

r001.rationale: The response explains how to assess the investment—distinguishing technological promise from returns, and examining valuations, debt, and investor dependence—before drawing its practical conclusion.

r002.rationale: It discusses rising prices and possible forced selling, but does not characterize a bubble as a large price rise followed by a collapse.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two questions: Is AI going to change the world? And will the investments being made in AI produce good returns at today’s prices? Those are very different questions.

A technology can be revolutionary and still be a bad investment if you pay too much for it. You can be right about the technology and wrong about the price.

So I would look at how much spending is taking place, how it’s being financed, and what earnings would have to materialize to justify the valuations. I’d also look at whether people are buying because they’ve carefully assessed those earnings, or because prices have gone up and they’re afraid of missing out.

Jeremy’s assessment is worth taking seriously. But identifying a bubble and knowing when it will end are different things. For an investor, the important question is: How exposed are you if those expectations turn out to be wrong?

r001.rationale: It lays out how to assess AI investment returns—spending, financing, required earnings, and investor behavior—instead of jumping straight to a conclusion.

r002.rationale: It mentions rising prices and uncertainty about when a bubble will end, but does not define a bubble as a large price rise followed by a collapse.
